links.note: 581 tells the ruler to hold spies and the reputed treatise as his eyes (இவையிரண்டும்... மன்னவன் கண்); 445 says a ruler proceeds with his counsellors as his eyes (சூழ்வார் கண்ணாக). Together they show the king's sight as something borrowed: spies, books and advisers each see for him where his own eyes do not reach.

392 calls numbers and letters, 'these two' (இவ்விரண்டும்), the eyes of living beings; 581 uses the same frame (இவையிரண்டும்... கண்) for the ruler's spies and treatise. The pairing shows the king's version adding to book-learning a second eye that 392 does not have: reports of what is actually happening.

582 makes it the king's work to know quickly, at all times (எஞ்ஞான்றும் வல்லறிதல்), all that happens to everyone; 553 says a ruler who does not inquire daily and do justice (நாடொறும் நாடி முறைசெய்யா) loses his land day by day. 553 gives the purpose and the cost: the daily knowing of 582 exists to feed daily justice, and its absence is paid for in the kingdom itself.

520 tells the king to look daily (நாடோறும் நாடுக) into the one doing his work, since the world stays straight if he does; 582 makes constant, quick knowledge of everyone's affairs the king's own occupation (வேந்தன் தொழில்). Both treat continuous inquiry, not occasional inspection, as the core of rule; 582 widens the object from the king's officers to everyone.

583 denies victory to a ruler who has things spied out but does not discern their meaning (ஒற்றிப் பொருள்தெரியா); 423 defines understanding as seeing the true substance of whatever is heard from anyone (அப்பொருள் மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது). The pairing shows the spy chapter applying the general rule about hearsay to intelligence: collecting reports is not yet knowing.

584 defines the spy as one who examines everyone, beginning with those who do the king's work (வினைசெய்வார்); 514 observes that even people trusted after every test often turn different through the nature of the work (வினைவகையான் வேறாகும்). 514 supplies the reason for watching one's own appointed officers: the testing done before appointment does not settle how they behave afterwards.

584 puts the king's own kin (தம் சுற்றம்) among those a spy examines, alongside his enemies (வேண்டாதார்); 882 says not to fear enemies who are like a sword but to fear the tie with enemies who are like kin (கேள்போல் பகைவர்). The chapter on internal enmity explains why 584 does not exempt relatives from scrutiny.

510 says that doubting a person one has examined and trusted (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும்) brings unending trouble; 584 has spies examine everyone (அனைவரையும் ஆராய்வது), including the king's own officers. The conflict holds if standing surveillance of appointed officers counts as the ஐயுறவு that 510 forbids; if spying is read as routine inquiry and not suspicion of a particular person, the two can stand together.

585 requires of a spy an unsuspected appearance, not flinching before eyes (கண்ணஞ்சாது) and never letting anything out; 686 requires of an envoy that he not fear the eye (கண் அஞ்சான்), which Parimelazhagar glosses in both verses as the angry look of the other side. The open agent and the covert one are given the same nerve; what differs is that the envoy must speak so it goes home, and the spy must give nothing away.

585 ends with the spy's ability never to let anything spill (யாண்டும் உகாஅமை); 689 wants the bearer of a king's message to be a hard man whose mouth does not let slip a damaging word (the edition prints வாய்சேரா; Parimelazhagar reads வாய் சோரா). Both make control of what leaves the mouth under pressure the test of the king's agents abroad.

276 says none are more hard-hearted than those who, unrenounced at heart, live by deceiving in the likeness of renouncers (துறந்தார்போல் வஞ்சித்து வாழ்வார்); 586 has the spy take the guise of renouncers (துறந்தார் படிவத்தராகி) to get into places and investigate. The conflict holds if 276 condemns the false ascetic guise as such; Parimelazhagar narrows 276 to cheating donors, and on that reading the spy's disguise in the king's service falls outside it.

274 likens doing what is not austerity under cover of austerity (தவமறைந்து) to a hunter hiding in a bush to snare birds; 586 describes the spy entering in an ascetic's form to find things out. The same figure, the ascetic's dress as a hide, is a reproach in the Book of Virtue and a working method in the Book of Wealth.

587 defines the spy as able to learn what was concealed and to hold what he has learned without doubt (ஐயப்பாடு இல்லதே); 702 ranks with a god the one who knows without doubt what is within another (ஐயப்படாஅது அகத்தது உணர்வானை). Both prize certain knowledge of what others hide, one gained by inquiry among informants and the other by reading a person's mind from signs.

695 tells those who serve a king not to listen in on or press after anything when a secret (மறை) is in progress, and to hear it only when he releases it; 587 makes the ability to hear concealed things (மறைந்தவை கேட்க வற்றாகி) the definition of a spy. The pairing marks a boundary: prying into secrets is a skill the king directs at others, and a fault when his own attendants turn it on him.

588 says that even what one spy found and brought should be confirmed through another spy (மற்றுமோர் ஒற்றினால்); 589 adds that spies should be run so that one does not know of another, and that what three say in agreement is to be accepted (மூவர் சொற்றொக்க தேறப்படும்). 589 turns the second opinion of 588 into a procedure: sources kept independent, and a threshold of agreement.

587 requires the spy to be free of doubt about what he has learned (அறிந்தவை ஐயப்பாடு இல்லதே); 588 tells the king to check even such a report (தந்த பொருளையும்) through another spy. The spy's certainty is a quality of the source and not a warrant for the king, who is to keep doubting until reports agree.

509 says to trust no one without examining and, after examining, to trust what is to be trusted (தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக); 589 says to run spies unknown to one another and to accept what three say in agreement (தேறப்படும்). Both give the same two-step rule, test first and then commit, 509 for persons and 589 for reports.

590 warns that a king who honours a spy so that others know of it (சிறப்பறிய) has himself let the secret out (புறப்படுத்தான் ஆகும் மறை); 663 says a deed should be done so that it shows only at the end, since showing midway brings lasting trouble (இடைக்கொட்கின்). In both the actor's own conduct, not an enemy's skill, is what exposes the undertaking.

440 says that if a ruler can enjoy what he loves without others knowing of his love (காதல் அறியாமை), his enemies' schemes come to nothing; 590 forbids showing favour to a spy where others can know of it. Both treat a ruler's visible attachments and rewards as information that others can use against him.

430 says those with understanding have everything and those without it have nothing whatever they have (என்னுடையரேனும் இலர்); 591 says energy is what makes one 'a haver' and asks whether those without it have even what they have (உடையது உடையரோ). The same formula is used of two different faculties, அறிவு and ஊக்கம், each presented as the thing that makes other possessions count.

1005 says those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing even with crores piled up (கோடியுண்டாயினும் இல்); 591 asks whether those without energy really have what they have. Both separate holding goods from having them, 1005 by the test of use and 591 by the test of the holder's drive.

400 calls learning the undecaying wealth and says other things are not wealth (மாடல்ல மற்றையவை); 592 calls possession of the inner drive the real possession and says possession of goods does not stay (நில்லாது நீங்கிவிடும்). Each chapter claims the title of lasting wealth for its own subject by the same contrast with goods that leave.

333 says wealth has the nature of not staying (அற்கா இயல்பிற்று) and concludes that on getting it one should at once do what stays; 592 also says goods do not stay (நில்லாது நீங்கிவிடும்) and concludes that the lasting possession is the inner drive (உள்ளம் உடைமை). Starting from the same fact, the Book of Virtue points to enduring deeds and the Book of Wealth to an inner resource that can make wealth again.

593 says those who hold steady energy as their cash in hand do not fret 'we have lost our gains' (இழந்தேமென்று அல்லாவார்); 626 asks whether those who never clutched at wealth saying 'we have got it' would grieve saying 'we have lost it' (அற்றேமென்று அல்லற்படுபவோ). Both describe calm at the loss of wealth through the loser's quoted words, but give different grounds: 593 a possession that remains, 626 the absence of clinging to begin with.

594 says prosperity itself asks the way and goes to the one of unwavering energy (அசைவிலா ஊக்கம்); 371 says unwavering effort (அசைவின்மை) itself arises from the fate that brings wealth, as sloth does from the fate that takes it. They share the word அசைவு and reverse its place: in 594 steadiness is the cause that draws prosperity, while in 371, read as it stands, steadiness is an effect of a gain already fated.

179 has Fortune, knowing the way (திறனறிந்து), go to those who know virtue and do not covet; 594 has prosperity ask the road (அதர்வினாய்) and go to the one of unwavering energy. The figure of wealth travelling by itself to its proper owner is used in the Book of Virtue for restraint and in the Book of Wealth for drive.

617 says the lotus goddess lives in the effort of the unslothful (மடியிலான் தாளுளாள்); 594 says prosperity finds its own way to the person of unwavering energy. Both personify fortune as choosing where it lives by the person's exertion, and neither leaves it to chance.

396 says a sand-well yields water as far as it is dug, and understanding as far as one has learned (தொட்டனைத்து... கற்றனைத்து); 595 says a water-flower's stem is as long as the water is deep, and a person's height as great as their inner drive (வெள்ளத்தனைய... உள்ளத்தனையது). Both use a water image and the same 'as much as' construction to state a strict proportion, one for learning and knowledge, the other for drive and stature.

596 says to aim at height in all one thinks, and that the aim, even if thrust aside, has the quality of not being thrust aside (தள்ளினும் தள்ளாமை நீர்த்து); 772 says holding the spear that missed an elephant is sweeter than the arrow that hit a forest hare. Both rate a high aim that fails above a low aim that succeeds, 596 as a rule of thought and 772 as a warrior's boast.

619 says that even if a thing cannot come about because of fate (தெய்வத்தான் ஆகாதெனினும்), effort pays the wage of the body's strain; 596 says a high aim keeps its worth even when it is thrust aside, which Parimelazhagar takes as being denied by fate. Both hold that what fate withholds in outcome does not cancel the value of the striving or the aim.

597 makes the bull elephant that holds its ground under arrows (பட்டுப்பாடு ஊன்றும் களிறு) the model of the strong-minded in ruin; 599 says the elephant, for all its bulk and sharp tusks, takes fright when a tiger attacks (வெரூஉம்). Within one chapter the same animal stands first for steadiness and then for size without spirit, so the reader cannot take the elephant as a simple emblem of either.

774 shows a warrior who has thrown his spear at an elephant pulling out the spear lodged in his own body and laughing; 597 shows the elephant itself holding firm when struck by arrows, as the image of those who do not give way in ruin. In both, a wound taken is the occasion that shows firmness, and the Book of Wealth draws the general rule in 597 that the war chapter acts out in 774.

613 says the pride called beneficence rests on the quality called effort (தாளாண்மை... வேளாண்மை என்னுஞ் செருக்கு); 598 says those without inner drive never reach the pride of saying 'we are generous' (வள்ளியம் என்னுஞ் செருக்கு). Both use செருக்கு approvingly for the giver's pride and make it depend on the giver's own exertion, stated positively in 613 and negatively in 598.

598 says the person without drive does not attain the pride of generosity; 614 says the beneficence of one without effort comes to nothing, like a sword in the hand of a பேடி. 614 adds what happens when such a person tries anyway: the means are present but the capacity to use them is not.

599 says an elephant, though huge and sharp-tusked, fears when a tiger attacks; 763 says a sea of roaring rats perishes when the cobra merely breathes. Both animal pairs teach that bulk or numbers do not decide a contest against an opponent with spirit, 599 of a person's drive and 763 of an army.

500 says a jackal kills the fearless elephant (கண்ணஞ்சா... களிறு) in mud where its legs sink; 599 says the elephant fears the tiger despite its size and tusks. Read together, the elephant loses in 599 for want of spirit and in 500 despite having it, so drive, which chapter 60 treats as decisive, is itself limited by the ground one fights on.

600 says a person's strength is abundance of the inner drive (உள்ள வெறுக்கை) and those without it are trees; 971 says a person's radiance is the same உள்ள வெறுக்கை and their disgrace is saying 'we will live without it'. The rare phrase recurs in the chapters on energy and on greatness, giving one quality as the source of both firmness and honour.

997 says those without human courtesy are like trees even if sharp as a file (மரம்போல்வர்); 600 says those without abundance of drive are trees, differing only in having human form (மரம் மக்களாதலே வேறு). The tree marks the person who lacks what makes one human, but the two verses name different lacks: fellow-feeling in 997, inner drive in 600.

576 says those who have eyes but do not extend kindly regard are like trees joined to the soil (மண்ணோடியைந்த மரத்தனையர்); 600 calls those without inner drive trees in human shape. In both the tree stands for something that has the outward parts but not the responsiveness or movement that should go with them.
